doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: European tours and the business of touring
summary: Small-town European jazz societies, and his aim to work less and be paid more.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: wants to come in for one night, most of these jazz parties won’t even allow them to buy a ticket for a night. In fact I’ve been really bucking to get them to change that. Or if they’re undersold, why not go to the local high school or college and give away a table to the best students or something, and get them to come in. It doesn’t cost anything. But it’s hard to get them to do that. Because it is a party, it’s their thing, so I think this particular thing may not last much longer. But there’s always new venues. There’s always individual people that like the music enough that they decide to put on concerts because nobody else will. There’s a lot of that in Europe. I do tours through England and Germany for example. We play small towns where you would never expect this music to be heard. And it’s always one person, just like these jazz parties, there’s always like one person who loves the music so much that they want to present it to everybody else. So you can build up a nice tour of 30 dates or so, that are all these small little jazz societies.

Are you enough of a let’s say business person that you’re able to look at a tour and figure here’s what I’m going to gross, how much is it going to cost me for everything else, and then go ahead and do it?

Yeah. I am now more and more. I mean my goal — this may sound like I’m just going for the money but it’s not really — I want to work less and be paid more. Because I want to be more and more controlling of the kind of music that I play. And it’s gradually reaching that stage. I’ll play festivals in Europe where they have enough money to bring over the whole band. And then once you can get everybody over there, on the festival’s plane ticket for example, you can do smaller dates with those guys. And you lose a little bit of money yourself. I’d rather make a little bit less and have the music completely the way I want it. So it’s always a give and take. Or I’ll use, I can do a pops concert or something and make quite a bit of money and then funnel that into sending out a bunch of promotional things to get more jobs for the group. As long as you’re still ahead, you’re doing okay. And my wife is very supportive of all this too you know. She says look as long as we’re eating and living, you do what you want to do.
